text: Today is your hundredth birthday. Your knees feel thirty, your bank account just doubled, and everyone from your graduation is dead.
You've got nine hundred years left. So what gives out first: your body, your money, or your mind?
Stay with me to the end. You'll find a diary you don't remember writing, and its first line will stop you cold.
It starts this morning. You wake up in your own bed, look in the mirror, and see the face you had at thirty.
No gray hair. No wrinkles. Doctors call it a miracle, and now they want your blood tested every single week.
Your cells stopped aging, so the clock should be frozen. But age was never the only thing that wears you down.
Think of a car that never rusts. It still drives every day, and every day the tires lose a little rubber.
That's your body now. It never gets old, but damage keeps piling up. And three parts are about to fail.
Year one hundred fifty. You bite into a cold apple and feel a sharp zing shoot through one tooth.
Enamel is the hard shell on your teeth. Once it wears away, your body never grows it back.
Every coffee, every crunch, every night of grinding scrapes off a little more. After a century, that shell is paper thin.
Then comes the second problem. Remember that loud concert at twenty? Your ears do, and they're still paying for it.
Deep inside your ear are tiny hair cells that turn sound into signals. Loud noise kills them, and they never grow back.
Year by year, the world gets quieter. By two hundred, you're laughing along at jokes you can't actually hear.
Now your eyes. The lens inside them never stops growing, layer after layer, like an onion that never gets peeled.
It gets thicker and cloudier, until the whole world looks like you're staring through a foggy window.
You pick up a menu at a diner. The words smear, so you hold it farther away, then farther still.
Teeth, ears, eyes. Three tiny parts, and they steal your senses one by one while the rest of you feels perfect.
Doctors have a name for it: wear, not age. Your heart is strong, but some parts can never be replaced.
Your body isn't old. It's just worn out.
Year two hundred. Your savings have sat in a bank this whole time, and the interest is wild.
Here's proof it works. In seventeen ninety, Benjamin Franklin left one thousand pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia.
His one rule was simple: don't touch it for two hundred years, and let it grow.
In nineteen ninety, Boston's fund had grown to roughly five million dollars, from one small gift.
You've got a thousand years of compound interest. So you must be the richest human who ever lived, right?
Wrong. The dollar only appeared in seventeen ninety-two, so your oldest savings would have to start in some other currency.
Even the British pound, the oldest money still in use today, is only about twelve hundred years old.
Empires print money, and empires collapse. Every few centuries, your fortune turns into paper nobody wants.
One morning you wake up with a suitcase of banknotes from a country that no longer exists.
A bank teller laughs, and you try to explain. She slides your entire life savings back across the counter.
So you start over. Again. Every few hundred years you build a fortune, and history deletes it.
You'll outlive the money before the money outlives you.
Year three hundred. Your phone holds a hundred and fifty contacts, about the most friendships one human brain can handle.
Scientists call it Dunbar's number. It's the size of the crowd your brain can truly keep track of.
But your crowd keeps shrinking. Every few years, you put on the same black suit and walk into another funeral.
Every few decades, your entire circle of friends is replaced. New faces, new names, new inside jokes to learn.
And at some point, you stop learning their names. Why bother, when they'll be gone in a blink?
A girl you loved at two hundred smiles at you from an old photo. You can't remember her last name.
The sad part is that you're not forgetting out of cruelty. It's self-defense.
Then there's family. Say you have four kids, and each of them has four kids, generation after generation.
Ten generations later, on paper, that's more than one million people walking around with your genes.
A million descendants, scattered across the planet, and you couldn't pick a single one of them out of a crowd.
You're the ancestor of an entire town you'll never meet. Somebody in it has your nose, and has no idea.
At a coffee shop, a stranger laughs exactly like your late brother. A distant grandson, maybe. You just walk past.
You can't tell him. He'd call a doctor. So you carry the whole family tree alone.
A long life gives you a family too big to hold, and too far away to touch.
Year five hundred. Here's something strange. Most neurons in your cortex, the thinking layer of your brain, are as old as you.
They're never replaced. So your brain is five hundred years old, and it's running out of room.
The oldest memories go first. Your first century slips away like a dream you can't retell after breakfast.
You try to picture your first love, your first car, your first apartment. All you see is a blur.
A neighbor asks about your childhood. You answer with a story you've told so often it's no longer a memory.
But your brain isn't your only problem. If you never age, there's only one thing left that can kill you: accidents.
A car crash. A fall. A slip in the shower. Each year, the odds are tiny. Over centuries, they pile up.
Year six hundred and fifty. You check the stairs twice. You stop driving. You stop swimming. You stop trusting ladders.
Your heart pounds every time a delivery truck honks outside. Your body wants to live very, very badly.
So you lock the front door and stay inside. For eighty years, you don't step out once.
You've beaten death, and the cure looks exactly like a prison.
Year seven hundred fifty. You finally step outside, and nobody understands a single word you say.
A thousand years ago, English sounded like Beowulf, an epic poem that today looks like a foreign language.
Languages drift. Every generation shifts a few sounds, until two people can't understand each other at all.
So you speak a dead dialect. You tell your best joke, and the whole room just stares at you.
Nobody gets your sayings. Nobody knows your references. You're the loneliest foreigner on Earth, and you never left home.
But the world isn't done with you yet. One last milestone is coming, and it's a big one.
July Fourth, twenty-seven seventy-six. The United States turns one thousand years old, and fireworks fill the sky above the city.
That's twice as old as the Mona Lisa. You're standing inside the history that everyone else only reads about.
Still, you're not the oldest thing around. In California's mountains, the oldest bristlecone pines are about forty-eight hundred years old.
They sprouted around the time the first great pyramids rose in Egypt, and they're still standing.
You rest a hand on the rough bark. For once in your life, you're the young one.
Your thousandth birthday arrives with a cake. One thousand candles, and the smoke alarm screams before you even blow.
Later that night, you're cleaning out a closet. At the bottom sits a dusty box older than most countries.
Inside is a leather diary in handwriting you don't recognize. Every page is full of names and dates.
Whole decades you can't remember. People you loved, and people you hated, and you've never heard of any of them.
You open the first page. In faded ink, the first line says: Today is my hundredth birthday.
Your hands start to shake. You hold it up to the light, and slowly you realize whose handwriting this is.
It's yours. You wrote it, and then you forgot it, just like you forgot everything else.
So tell me in the comments: if you lived to a thousand, what would break first, your body, your money, or your mind?
